can-wood-borer-bees-sting-what-mesa-home.title: Can Wood Borer Bees Sting? What Mesa Homeowners Should Know About Carpenter Bee Stings
can-wood-borer-bees-sting-what-mesa-home.excerpt: Wood borer bees are carpenter bees. Females can sting but rarely do, and males have no stinger. Here is who stings, what to do, and when to call us in Mesa.
can-wood-borer-bees-sting-what-mesa-home.content:
Yes, wood borer bees can sting, but only the females, and they rarely do. Wood borer bees are carpenter bees, and the males you see hovering and dive-bombing near your Mesa eaves have no stinger at all. A female will sting only if she is grabbed, stepped on or has her nest disturbed. If a nest is above a door, patio seat or play area, call us at (480) 422-8388 and we will inspect it through our bee and wasp removal in Mesa service.

We field this question from homeowners all over Mesa, ZIP codes 85201 through 85210, from the older ranch homes near downtown Mesa to the stucco patios around Dobson Ranch, Red Mountain and Las Sendas. The story is nearly always the same: a big, shiny insect hangs in the air a foot from someone's face on the back patio, and the family wonders whether it is about to sting. Most of the time the answer is no, and knowing why saves a lot of worry. This guide is about the sting question itself. If you want the full removal and prevention walk-through for carpenter bees, our Tempe carpenter bee guide covers it in detail.

Which Wood Borer Bees Can Sting and Which Cannot?

Only female carpenter bees can sting. Males have no stinger, so their aggressive hovering and head-height buzzing is bluff. Females carry a stinger but are docile and mostly ignore people unless they are handled or trapped. Honey bees and wasps behave very differently, and that difference is what matters at your house.

InsectCan it sting?How it behaves near peopleWhat it usually means
Male carpenter beeNo, no stingerHovers, darts at you, bumps into youA nest is nearby, but he cannot hurt you
Female carpenter beeYes, rarely doesStays near the hole, ignores peopleSting only if grabbed, stepped on or cornered
Honey beeYesDefends a hive in numbersA colony in a wall or tree needs professional removal
Paper waspYes, repeatedlyDefends an open umbrella-shaped nestNest under eaves or patio covers
Bumble beeYes, if provokedQuiet, feeds on flowersUsually ground or cavity nests

The practical takeaway: a hovering bee that looks big and angry is far more likely to be a male carpenter bee than anything dangerous.

Why Do Carpenter Bees Dive-Bomb You If the Males Cannot Sting?

Males guard the nesting area. In spring they patrol the eaves, fascia boards and pergola beams where females drill, and they investigate anything that moves, including your head. They are also trying to mate, and they chase off rivals. It looks threatening, but it is territorial display. You can walk through it, though it is fair to say it is unnerving.

Here is what we tell customers to look for:

  • Hovering in one spot. A male holding position in front of a beam is guarding. A colony defender would fly straight at you and in numbers.
  • One or two bees, not a cloud. Carpenter bees are solitary. A swarm or a steady stream in and out of one opening points to honey bees or wasps.
  • A clean round hole. A half-inch circular entrance in bare wood with sawdust below is the signature of a carpenter bee nest.
  • Bare, shiny abdomen. Bumble bees have a fuzzy back end. Carpenter bees usually have a smooth, shiny one.

When Does a Female Carpenter Bee Actually Sting?

A female stings in defense, and only after a lot of provocation. She is busy digging a gallery and provisioning cells with pollen. If you leave her alone she leaves you alone. The cases we see in Mesa are almost always a person who swatted one, grabbed one with a bare hand, or pushed a finger or tool into the hole.

Situations that raise the risk:

  • Reaching into a nest hole to clear sawdust or plug it with your fingers.
  • Swatting at a bee that has landed on your arm or shirt.
  • Barefoot contact on a patio where a bee has dropped or is crawling.
  • Working directly on a ladder beside an active gallery.
  • Children or pets poking at the hole.

Carpenter bees also have strong mandibles for chewing wood, so you may hear them described as biting. In our experience that is rare, and it happens only when one is held.

What Should You Do If You or a Family Member Is Stung?

Move away from the nest, wash the area with soap and water, and apply a cold pack to reduce swelling. A single carpenter bee sting usually causes brief pain and a small red bump. Watch closely for the first 30 minutes. Any trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, hives across the body or dizziness is an emergency: call 911.

A short checklist:

  1. Step back from the nest area and keep children and pets away.
  2. Wash the sting with soap and water.
  3. Use a cold pack on the area for short periods.
  4. Stay with the person and watch for any spreading swelling or breathing changes.
  5. Call 911 for signs of a severe allergic reaction.
  6. Call your doctor or pharmacist for questions about pain or itching relief.

We are pest control technicians, not medical providers, so for anyone with a known bee allergy, follow the plan their doctor gave them.

How Can You Tell Whether It Is a Carpenter Bee Problem or Something More Serious?

Check the entrance, the numbers and the sound. A single round hole with a lone bee points to a carpenter bee. Many insects moving through a crack, a humming from inside a wall, or a papery nest hanging from the eave points to honey bees or wasps, which sting far more readily.

What you seeMost likelySting risk
Round half-inch hole, sawdust below, one or two beesCarpenter beeLow
Steady stream of bees entering a wall crack or tree hollowHoney bee colonyHigh if disturbed
Open gray paper nest under eave or patio coverPaper waspsHigh if disturbed
Bees ignoring you, feeding on bloomsForaging beesLow
Sawdust-like frass plus tiny exit holes in structural woodPossible termites or other wood borersNone, but needs inspection

If you are not sure, take a photo from a safe distance and send it with your service request. A wasp nest on the same patio is a separate problem; our wasp nest safety guide explains why you should never spray one from a ladder.

Where Do Carpenter Bees Nest on Mesa Homes?

They choose bare, dry, softer wood: fascia boards, eave undersides, pergola beams, wooden fence rails, patio covers and unpainted door trim. In our part of the Valley, sun-dried and weathered wood is especially attractive. Painted or stained surfaces are far less appealing.

The spots we check first on a Mesa inspection:

  • Fascia and rafter tails on the south and west sides of the house.
  • Wood patio covers and ramadas common in backyards around Dobson Ranch and Red Mountain.
  • Pergolas and shade structures with exposed beams.
  • Wooden fence posts and gates.
  • Old, dry palm trunks and agave stalks.

Look at where people sit. A nest directly over a patio table or beside a front door is the one to address first because that is where an accidental sting could happen.

Do Carpenter Bees Damage Wood and Do They Need Treatment?

One hole is minor, but a gallery reused and extended year after year can weaken fascia, rafters and beams, and woodpeckers sometimes tear the wood apart to get at the larvae. Carpenter bees do not eat wood the way termites do. They chew it out and push the sawdust away. If you see a lot of sawdust and many holes, it is worth having a professional look.

What actually helps:

  • Treat the gallery, then plug the hole only after the bees have left.
  • Paint or stain exposed wood so new bees skip it.
  • Replace rotted trim with hardwood, vinyl or metal where practical.
  • Do not seal a live nest, because trapped bees may chew a new way out.

Is It Safe to Spray a Carpenter Bee Hole Yourself?

For a single, small nest at ground level, many homeowners do it. The danger is working from a ladder beside an active gallery, or using the wrong product. Always follow the label, wear eye protection and gloves, and keep kids and pets away. If the nest is high, over a doorway, or you are allergic to stings, leave it to a technician.

SituationDIY reasonable?Better to call a pro
One hole at ground level, no allergiesOftenIf it returns
Nest on a second-story fasciaNoYes, ladder risk
Many holes across the same beamNoYes, repeat nesting
Anyone in the home allergic to stingsNoYes
Not sure it is a carpenter beeNoYes, identify first

What About Carpenter Bees and Stings in Nearby Cities?

The same biology applies across the East Valley. We handle bee problems in Gilbert, Chandler, Tempe, Apache Junction and Gold Canyon, and each city's housing differs a bit. If you are in Gilbert, see our bee and wasp removal in Gilbert. In Chandler, our bee and wasp removal in Chandler page applies, and our Chandler bumble bee sting guide compares more bee types. For a complete look at our service in the city, start with pest control and termite treatment in Mesa, and for a real removal example in the area read our Mesa hive extraction article.

Scorpions are the other stinging pest Mesa homeowners worry about, and the sting is a different matter entirely, so we cover it on our scorpion control in Mesa page.

Frequently Asked Questions About Wood Borer Bee Stings in Mesa

Can wood borer bees sting?

Yes, but only females, and rarely. Wood borer bees are carpenter bees. Males have no stinger, and females sting mostly when handled or trapped.

Do carpenter bees bite?

They have strong jaws for chewing wood and can nip if held, but that is uncommon. They do not go after people.

Why is a big bee flying at my face?

That is almost always a male guarding a nest. He has no stinger, and the display is territorial.

Are carpenter bee stings dangerous?

For most people a sting is brief and mild. Anyone with a bee allergy, or who has trouble breathing or facial swelling, should call 911.

Should I kill a carpenter bee on sight?

Not needed for safety. Focus on the nest and the wood. If a nest is by a doorway or patio seat, have it treated.

Do you remove carpenter bees in Mesa?

Yes. We serve 85201 through 85210. Call (480) 422-8388 or request service online.

how-can-you-get-rid-of-termites-what-avo.title: How Can You Get Rid of Termites? What Avondale Homeowners Should Know About Treating Subterranean Termites
how-can-you-get-rid-of-termites-what-avo.excerpt: Get rid of termites by treating the colony, not the visible insects. Here is what works in Avondale, what does not, and when to call a licensed technician.
how-can-you-get-rid-of-termites-what-avo.content:
The most reliable way to get rid of termites is to confirm which kind you have and then treat the soil around the foundation or place bait stations, because spraying the termites you can see never reaches the colony. In Avondale that colony is usually desert subterranean termites living in the ground, so a professional liquid barrier or baiting system is the fix that holds. If you have found mud tubes or swarmers, call us at (480) 422-8388 and we will inspect through our termite treatment in Avondale service.

Homeowners across Avondale, ZIP codes 85323 and 85392, ask us this after the same kind of discovery: a pencil-wide dirt tube climbing a stucco wall in Garden Lakes, a cloud of winged insects at a window in Coldwater Springs after a monsoon storm, or a soft spot in a baseboard in an older home near Historic Avondale. Avondale sits along the Agua Fria River, and the irrigated yards, canals and farm-edge soil around it give termites the moisture they need. This guide walks through what actually works, what only looks like it works, and when to stop experimenting and call a licensed technician.

How Can You Get Rid of Termites in an Avondale Home?

You get rid of termites by removing the colony, not the visible insects. For subterranean termites that means a continuous treated zone in the soil around and under the structure, or bait stations that workers carry back to the colony. For drywood termites it means localized treatment of the infested wood. Both start with an inspection that identifies the species and maps where the activity is.

Here is the order we follow at a typical Avondale house:

  1. Identify the termite. Mud tubes and soil-colored swarmers point to subterranean termites. Tiny six-sided pellets that look like sand point to drywood termites.
  2. Map the activity. We check the slab edge, stucco weep screed, garage walls, pipe penetrations, wood fences and any wood touching soil.
  3. Choose the treatment. A liquid barrier, a baiting system, spot treatment or a combination, depending on the species and the house.
  4. Fix the conditions. Moisture, soil contact and stored wood are what invited them in, so those get corrected too.
  5. Re-inspect. Termites can return from a neighboring colony, so follow-up inspections matter more than the first visit.

What Kind of Termites Do Avondale Homes Get?

Avondale homes mostly get desert subterranean termites, with occasional drywood termites in furniture, attic framing and eaves. The two behave differently, and the right treatment depends entirely on which one you have.

TypeWhere it livesTelltale signUsual treatment approach
SubterraneanColony in the soil, travels to wood through mud tubesPencil-wide mud tubes on foundation or stucco, swarmers after rainLiquid soil barrier or bait stations around the structure
DrywoodLives entirely inside dry wood, no soil contactSmall sand-like pellets below kick-out holesLocalized treatment of the affected wood
Flying ants (not termites)Ant nests in soil or wallsPinched waist, bent antennae, unequal wing pairsAnt control, not termite treatment

Not sure whether the winged insects at your window are termites or ants? Our Phoenix guide to termites that look like flying ants and our Mesa termite identification guide show the differences side by side.

Do Home Remedies Get Rid of Termites?

Home remedies can kill the termites they touch, but they almost never eliminate a colony. Subterranean termites live in the soil and workers stay out of sight, so a spray, foam or sprinkled powder reaches a tiny fraction of them while the rest keep feeding.

  • Orange oil and vinegar sprays: surface contact only. They do not travel through wood or soil.
  • Boric acid and borate on bare wood: can protect untreated wood during construction, but will not stop a soil colony.
  • Store-bought foam and aerosol cans: useful on a visible drywood kick-out hole, not on a mud tube network.
  • Sealing the tube: workers rebuild or reroute within days.

The real risk is that a failed DIY attempt can scatter the colony into new feeding areas and give you a false sense of security while the damage continues out of view.

What Are the Early Signs of Termites in Avondale?

The earliest signs are mud tubes, swarmers, discarded wings and hollow-sounding wood. Most Avondale homeowners notice one of these long before they see damage.

  • Mud tubes on the slab edge, garage wall, stucco or block wall.
  • Winged swarmers or piles of translucent wings near windows and doors, often after monsoon storms.
  • Baseboards or door frames that sound hollow or feel soft when tapped.
  • Paint that bubbles or wood that looks water-damaged with no leak.
  • Fine pellets collecting beneath a wood trim or window frame.

When do termites swarm in the Phoenix area? Swarms are most common after monsoon rain, from roughly July through September, and a swarm inside your home means a colony is already established nearby. Swarmers do not eat wood. They fly to start new colonies, so seeing them is a signal, not the damage itself.

Why Do Termites Show Up in Avondale Yards and Homes?

Termites are not a sign of a dirty house. They are a sign of food and moisture in the wrong place, and Avondale's mix of newer master-planned neighborhoods and older homes near the river gives them both in different forms. A fast-growing subdivision can have buried construction wood left under the slab, while an older lot may have decades of landscape changes piled against the wall.

Termites follow moisture and wood. Avondale's irrigated landscaping, canal-fed soil, and block-wall and stucco construction create plenty of both.

  • Soil against stucco: when landscaping or pavers cover the weep screed, termites get a hidden path into the wall.
  • Irrigation leaks and drip lines: constant moisture next to the slab draws colonies.
  • Stored wood and old stumps: firewood, lumber and dead roots feed colonies next to the house.
  • Older wood fences and pergolas: a fence post can be a bridge to the house.

How Do Professionals Treat for Termites?

Before any product goes down, a technician looks at how your particular house is built. A slab-on-grade home with a garage, a block wall tied into the stucco and a planter bed against the patio each creates a different entry point, and a good treatment plan follows those details instead of a generic checklist. That is why two Avondale neighbors on the same street can end up with different plans.

Professionals treat the soil or bait the colony. We offer both liquid barrier treatments and baiting systems, and the choice depends on the structure, the species and where the activity is.

MethodHow it worksBest for
Liquid soil barrierA treated zone in the soil around the foundation that termites cannot cross unharmedActive subterranean activity, slab homes
Baiting systemStations around the home that workers feed on and carry back to the colonyOngoing monitoring, sensitive areas
Spot or localized treatmentTreatment applied directly to infested woodDrywood termites in a limited area
Pre-construction treatmentSoil treatment before the slab is pouredNew builds and additions

For more detail on the service, see termite treatment in Avondale or the wider Avondale pest and termite control page.

How Can You Keep Termites From Coming Back?

Keep soil, wood and moisture away from your foundation and schedule regular inspections. Prevention is mostly habit, and most of it you can start this weekend.

  • Keep at least a few inches of the stucco weep screed visible above soil, gravel and pavers.
  • Fix drip-line and sprinkler leaks near the slab quickly.
  • Store firewood and lumber away from the house, off the ground.
  • Remove old stumps and wood debris from the yard.
  • Do not let wood fences or trellises touch the house.
  • Have the home inspected on a regular schedule, especially after monsoon season.

Are Termites in Nearby Cities Different?

The species are the same across the West Valley, but the construction and soil change. We also treat for termites in Goodyear, Litchfield Park, Buckeye, Glendale and Phoenix. A newer Garden Lakes or Rancho Santa Fe slab home and an older Historic Avondale house need different inspection priorities, even though the termite is the same.

Should You Worry About Other Pests Too?

Moisture and wood problems that attract termites often attract other pests, so a termite visit is a good time to ask about the rest. Avondale homeowners also deal with bark scorpions and ants, covered in our guides to scorpion stings in Avondale and ant control in Avondale.

Frequently Asked Questions About Getting Rid of Termites in Avondale

How can you get rid of termites?

Treat the colony, not the visible insects. For subterranean termites that means a soil barrier or bait stations around the structure. For drywood termites it means treating the infested wood.

Can I get rid of termites myself?

DIY products can kill the termites they touch but rarely reach the colony. A professional inspection is the only reliable way to know how far the activity goes.

How do I know if I have termites or flying ants?

Termites have straight antennae, a thick waist and wings of equal length. Flying ants have bent antennae, a pinched waist and unequal wings.

Do termites go away on their own?

No. A colony keeps feeding for as long as it has food and moisture, and the damage compounds quietly.

What should I do if I see swarmers in my house?

Do not spray. Save a few for identification, take photos, and call us so we can inspect.

Do you treat for termites in Avondale?

Yes. We serve 85323 and 85392. Call (480) 422-8388 or request service online.

crabgrass-vs-bermuda-grass-how-maricopa-.title: Crabgrass vs Bermuda Grass: How Maricopa Homeowners Can Tell Them Apart and Treat Each One
crabgrass-vs-bermuda-grass-how-maricopa-.excerpt: Crabgrass is a wide-bladed annual that dies each winter; Bermuda is a perennial that spreads by runners. Here is how to tell them apart in Maricopa.
crabgrass-vs-bermuda-grass-how-maricopa-.content:
Crabgrass is a summer annual weed with wide, light-green blades that grows in sprawling clumps and dies off when cold nights arrive, while Bermuda grass is a perennial with narrow, darker blades that spreads by runners and roots and comes back every spring. In Maricopa that difference decides the fix: crabgrass is stopped with a well-timed pre-emergent, and Bermuda where you do not want it needs repeated treatments through our Bermuda grass control in Maricopa. Call (480) 422-8388 if you are not sure which one you have.

We get this question from homeowners all over Maricopa, in ZIP codes 85138 and 85139, usually in late summer. A Bermuda lawn in Rancho El Dorado suddenly has coarse, pale patches. A backyard in Tortosa or Alterra has grass creeping out of the turf and into the gravel. A Province homeowner sees "grass" pushing up through rock in a front yard that was never supposed to have any. Some of it is crabgrass and some of it is Bermuda, and the two need opposite plans. This guide shows you how to tell them apart in a few minutes and what actually works on each one in Pinal County's heat.

What Is the Difference Between Crabgrass and Bermuda Grass?

The short answer: crabgrass lives one season and returns from seed, while Bermuda lives for years and returns from its own runners and roots. Crabgrass is a weed in any lawn. Bermuda is the most common lawn grass in the low desert, and it only becomes a weed when it spreads into gravel, flower beds or a neighbor's yard where nobody wants it.

  • Crabgrass (Digitaria species, mainly large and smooth crabgrass) is a warm-season annual. Each plant sprouts from seed in spring or summer, sets thousands of new seeds and dies when the cold arrives.
  • Bermuda grass (Cynodon dactylon) is a warm-season perennial. It spreads above ground by stolons (runners) and below ground by rhizomes, so one plant can travel several feet in a single summer.

Because one is an annual and the other is a perennial, the same treatment will not handle both. A pre-emergent that stops crabgrass seed does almost nothing to a Bermuda rhizome already in the ground.

How Do You Tell Crabgrass From Bermuda Grass?

Look at four things: blade width, growth shape, the spot where the blade meets the stem, and the seed head. Crabgrass blades are wide and flat and the plant grows outward from one center like the legs of a crab. Bermuda blades are thin, the turf forms a tight mat, and it spreads by both above-ground runners and underground rhizomes. Crabgrass stems can also root where they lie on the soil, so a rooted stem alone does not prove you have Bermuda. Use several traits together.

FeatureCrabgrassBermuda grass
Life cycleAnnual, returns from seedPerennial, returns from runners and rhizomes
Blade widthWide and flat, roughly a quarter inch or moreNarrow, about an eighth of an inch or less
ColorPale or yellow-green, stands out in a lawnMedium to deep green in summer
Growth shapeLow clump spreading out from one centerDense mat of runners plus underground rhizomes
Where blade meets stemThin papery collar (ligule), no hair ringSmall fringe of hairs
Seed headFinger-like spikes, often spaced slightly apart near the stem tip3 to 7 finger-like spikes fanning out from a single point
Winter look in MaricopaDies and leaves bare spotsGoes dormant and tan, greens up in spring
Best preventionPre-emergent before soil warmsEdging barriers plus repeated post-emergent treatment

Is the pull test a reliable way to check?

It is one useful clue, not a final answer. Grab the plant at the base and pull. A young crabgrass plant often lifts out as a clump with a shallow, fibrous root ball. Bermuda usually tears, and you may see a white underground stem (a rhizome) snapping off below the soil line. But older crabgrass can root at the joints of stems lying on the ground, so a plant that resists or has rooted stems is not automatically Bermuda. Before you decide, also check blade width, color, the hair ring or papery collar where the blade meets the stem, and the seed head shape from the table above.

Why do the seed heads look so alike?

Both grasses grow finger-shaped seed spikes, which is why so many people mix them up in August. On Bermuda the fingers all fan out from one point at the top of the stem, like the spokes of a small umbrella. On crabgrass they tend to be longer and are often staggered a little along the stem tip. Check the blade width and the growth shape too before you decide.

Why Does Crabgrass Show Up in Maricopa Bermuda Lawns?

Crabgrass moves into thin spots. When a Bermuda lawn has bare patches, frequent light watering and full sun on the soil surface, crabgrass seed has everything it needs. Maricopa yards check all three boxes for much of the year.

  • Thin turf after winter. Bermuda is still waking up from dormancy when crabgrass begins to sprout, so the weed gets a head start in any gap.
  • Short, frequent irrigation cycles. Daily shallow watering keeps the top inch of soil moist, which favors shallow-rooted crabgrass over deep-rooted Bermuda.
  • Monsoon moisture. Summer storms from July through September bring new flushes of summer weeds into lawns and gravel alike.
  • Seed from nearby open ground. Many Maricopa neighborhoods sit next to open desert, farm fields or vacant lots, and seed blows or washes in from the edges.

Why Does Bermuda Grass Keep Spreading Into Gravel?

Bermuda spreads into rock because its runners and rhizomes travel under borders and through landscape fabric seams, and the irrigation that keeps your lawn green also feeds the runners that escape it. Removing what you see above the gravel leaves the rhizomes alive, so it grows back within weeks.

This is the most common call we take from Maricopa homeowners with mixed yards: a small Bermuda lawn in the backyard and desert rock everywhere else. The fix is to treat the escaped Bermuda while it is actively growing, usually several times across the warm season, and to set up a clean edge so the lawn stops feeding new runners into the rock. Our guide to why Bermuda grass is so hard to kill explains the root system in more detail.

How Do You Get Rid of Crabgrass in a Bermuda Lawn?

Prevent the seed from sprouting, then remove the few that get through. A pre-emergent applied before soil temperatures reach the mid-50s Fahrenheit stops most crabgrass, and in the low desert that usually means a February application. Anything that sprouts later can be pulled while small or treated with a selective product labeled for crabgrass in Bermuda.

  1. Time the pre-emergent. It has to be in place before germination. Our pre-emergent weed control in Maricopa is scheduled around soil temperature, not the calendar alone. For the basics, see what a pre-emergent herbicide does.
  2. Pull or spot-treat young plants. A few small clumps can be pulled by hand while they are young. Lift any stems that have rooted at their joints along with the main clump, and bag plants that already carry seed heads. Larger outbreaks call for a selective post-emergent that spares the Bermuda.
  3. Thicken the Bermuda. Dense, well-fed turf shades the soil and leaves crabgrass nowhere to start.
  4. Water deeper and less often. Longer, less frequent cycles push Bermuda roots down and dry the surface where crabgrass seed sprouts.

Does pre-emergent hurt winter ryegrass?

It can. Many Maricopa lawns are overseeded with ryegrass in fall, and a pre-emergent put down at the wrong time will block the rye seed the same way it blocks weed seed. We plan the two together so the fall seed has room to establish and the spring pre-emergent goes down on schedule. If you overseed, read when to seed Bermuda grass before you set your calendar.

How Do You Get Rid of Bermuda Grass Where You Don't Want It?

Treat it during active summer growth, repeat the treatment as it regrows, and cut off its supply line from the lawn. Bermuda stores energy in rhizomes, so one application rarely finishes it. Expect a series of treatments across the warm season, with the biggest results when temperatures are high and the grass is green.

  • In gravel and rock: treatments that target everything green in the bed, applied carefully away from plants you want to keep.
  • In flower and shrub beds: selective grass treatments that leave broadleaf plants alone.
  • At the lawn edge: a physical edge or barrier deep enough to slow runners, plus regular treatment of anything that crosses it.

Our team handles the same problem across southern Arizona. See how we approach Bermuda grass removal in Casa Grande, our Pinal County neighbor, and Bermuda grass invasion in Sahuarita in Pima County.

When Do Crabgrass and Bermuda Grass Grow in Maricopa?

Both are warm-season grasses, so their busy months overlap, but their winter behavior is opposite. Use this calendar to match your treatment to what each plant is doing.

MonthsCrabgrassBermuda grassWhat we focus on
Jan to FebSeed waiting in the soilDormant, tanSpring pre-emergent before soil warms
Mar to MayFirst seedlings in thin spotsGreen-up, runners start movingSpot treatment, edge checks
Jun to SepPeak growth, seed heads, monsoon flushesPeak growth and spreadRepeat Bermuda treatment in gravel and beds
Oct to DecDies with cold nights, seed left behindSlows, heads into dormancyOverseeding plans, map bare spots for spring

What Does Professional Weed Control in Maricopa Include?

We start by identifying what is actually growing, because a crabgrass plan and a Bermuda plan look nothing alike. From there we combine pre-emergent and post-emergent treatments on a schedule built for low-desert soil temperatures and for whether you overseed in winter. We are a weed control and lawn treatment company, so our visits focus on the weeds and the turf's health.

Bucksworth Home Services has been locally owned since 2013 by Jordan and Taylor Moore and is based in Apache Junction. Our technicians work in Maricopa neighborhoods such as Rancho El Dorado, Province, Tortosa, Alterra, Glennwilde and Cobblestone Farms, from the homes near Copper Sky Recreation Complex out to the farm-edge streets by the Maricopa Agricultural Center. We also serve nearby Bermuda grass control in Casa Grande, as well as San Tan Valley, Laveen, Chandler and Coolidge. You can watch our crews at work on the Bucksworth YouTube channel.

Maricopa homeowners often ask about bugs while we are on the property, since the same irrigation and desert edges draw scorpions and ants. Our pest control in Maricopa covers those. When you are ready for weed help, call (480) 422-8388 or request service online.

Frequently Asked Questions About Crabgrass and Bermuda Grass

Is crabgrass the same as Bermuda grass?

No. Crabgrass is an annual weed with wide, pale blades that dies each winter. Bermuda is a perennial turfgrass with narrow blades that spreads by runners and rhizomes and returns every spring.

Does crabgrass die in the winter in Arizona?

Yes. Crabgrass dies when cold nights arrive in late fall, but it leaves seed in the soil that sprouts the next spring. That is why a spring pre-emergent matters even after the plants are gone.

Will a pre-emergent stop Bermuda grass?

Not established Bermuda. A pre-emergent only blocks seeds from sprouting, and spreading Bermuda grows from runners and rhizomes. It needs post-emergent treatment during active growth.

Can crabgrass take over a Bermuda lawn?

It can fill thin, overwatered areas fast in summer. A dense Bermuda lawn with deep, infrequent watering and a timed pre-emergent keeps crabgrass in check.

Why is there grass growing in my gravel yard?

In Maricopa it is usually Bermuda escaping from a nearby lawn, or crabgrass and other summer weeds sprouting after monsoon rain. Compare blade width, color, the collar where the blade meets the stem and the seed head; a pull test is one more clue but not proof on its own.

water-bugs-vs-cockroaches-how-gilbert-ho.title: Water Bugs vs Cockroaches: How Gilbert Homeowners Can Tell Them Apart and What to Do
water-bugs-vs-cockroaches-how-gilbert-ho.excerpt: Most "water bugs" in Gilbert homes are cockroaches. Here is how to tell a true water bug from a roach, why they come up drains, and what to do next.
water-bugs-vs-cockroaches-how-gilbert-ho.content:
A "water bug" in a Gilbert house is almost always a cockroach. True water bugs are aquatic insects that live in ponds and only end up indoors by accident, while the large dark "water bugs" people find in kitchens, bathrooms and garages are usually American or Oriental cockroaches coming up from drains, sewer lines and irrigation boxes. If you are seeing them inside more than once, our roach elimination in Gilbert treats where they live, not just where you spot them. Call (480) 422-8388.

We hear the phrase "water bug" all over Gilbert, from older homes near the Heritage District in 85233 and 85234 to newer streets in Morrison Ranch, Power Ranch, Seville and Agritopia in 85295, 85296, 85297 and 85298. The name sounds less alarming than "cockroach", and some people genuinely believe the big shiny insect in the laundry room is a different animal. Gilbert does have real water bugs, though. The ponds at the Riparian Preserve at Water Ranch, community lakes such as the ones in Val Vista Lakes, and backyard pools all give aquatic insects a place to live. This guide explains how to tell the two apart in a few seconds, why it matters for what you do next, and when a sighting means you have a roach problem.

What Is the Difference Between a Water Bug and a Cockroach?

They belong to different insect orders and live completely different lives. True water bugs (giant water bugs, sometimes called "toe biters") are aquatic predators in the order Hemiptera. They hunt tadpoles, small fish and insects underwater and breathe at the surface. Cockroaches are land scavengers in the order Blattodea that eat almost anything and shelter in dark, damp voids. A water bug that gets indoors is lost. A cockroach indoors is often looking for a place to stay.

The confusion comes from habits, not looks. American and Oriental cockroaches love moisture, so homeowners find them near sinks, tubs, floor drains and water heaters, and the nickname "water bug" stuck.

How Can You Tell a Water Bug From a Cockroach?

Check the antennae first, then the legs and body shape. Cockroaches have long, thread-like antennae that are often as long as the body. True water bugs have very short antennae tucked under the head, thick grasping front legs that look like small pincers, and a flatter, broader oval body built for swimming.

FeatureTrue water bugCockroach called a "water bug"
AntennaeShort, hidden under the headLong and thread-like, constantly moving
Front legsThick, hooked grasping legsSpiny running legs, all similar
MouthpartsPiercing beak for feeding on preyChewing mouthparts for scavenging
Body shapeBroad, flat ovalLonger oval with a shield-like plate behind the head
Where it livesPonds, lakes, slow water, sometimes poolsSewer lines, drains, irrigation and meter boxes, wall voids
How it gets insideFlies to lights at night and wanders in by accidentCrawls up drains and through gaps around pipes and doors
Bite riskCan give a painful bite if handledBites are very rare
Health concern indoorsLow; it cannot live in a houseContaminates food and surfaces, can trigger allergies

Is the big brown roach in my garage a water bug?

Almost certainly not. A reddish-brown roach about an inch and a half long with a pale, yellowish band around the plate behind its head is an American cockroach, the insect most often called a water bug. It runs fast, may fly short distances on hot nights, and usually comes from the sewer or a nearby utility box.

What about the shiny black ones?

A dark, almost black roach about an inch long that moves slowly is likely an Oriental cockroach. It favors cooler, wetter spots such as crawl spaces, floor drains and the soil under leaky hose bibs. In the Valley we also see Turkestan cockroaches outdoors in water meter and irrigation boxes, where the males are tan and the females are darker with short wings.

Which "Water Bugs" Do Gilbert Homeowners Actually Find?

Inside the house, our technicians find large cockroaches far more often than any aquatic insect. These are the usual suspects:

  • American cockroaches: the classic "water bug" in kitchens, bathrooms and garages, especially after warm nights.
  • Oriental cockroaches: slow, dark roaches near floor drains, laundry rooms and damp slab edges.
  • Turkestan cockroaches: outdoor roaches in irrigation valve boxes, block wall gaps and mulch, which wander in under doors.
  • German cockroaches: small, tan roaches that live indoors near appliances. Nobody calls these water bugs, but they are the hardest to clear. Our German cockroach guide from Mesa covers them in detail.

Outside, a true giant water bug usually shows up in one of two places: floating in the pool skimmer, or on the patio under a porch light near a lake or pond. That is why homes close to the Riparian Preserve, Freestone Park and the lake communities see them more than homes in the middle of a dry subdivision.

Why Are Cockroaches Called Water Bugs?

Because the roaches that get the name live where water is. American and Oriental cockroaches need moisture and spend their lives in sewers, storm drains and damp utility spaces, then show up beside sinks and tubs. The nickname also softens the news. "We had a water bug" sounds better to a guest than "we have roaches", so the term has hung on for generations.

The trouble is that the softer name can delay a fix. A roach that came up a drain once can come back the same way, and an occasional "water bug" can turn into a steady stream when the weather heats up.

Why Do Water Bugs Come Up Through Drains in Gilbert?

Most do not come up through the drain itself. They usually come from the sewer side or from gaps around plumbing where pipes enter walls and slabs. In Gilbert we see three common entry patterns:

  1. Dry drain traps. A guest shower, laundry sink or floor drain that sits unused can lose the water in its trap and give roaches an open path from the sewer.
  2. Gaps around plumbing. Openings around pipes under sinks, behind toilets and at the water heater connect wall voids to living space.
  3. Outdoor harborage near the house. Irrigation valve boxes, water meter boxes, cleanouts and pool equipment pads stay damp all summer and hold roaches right next to the slab.

The East Valley's long hot season keeps sewer roach activity high from late spring through fall, and warm nights bring them to the surface. Monsoon storms can also push them out of flooded underground spaces and toward homes.

Are Water Bugs Dangerous?

A true water bug can bite hard if you pick it up, and the bite is painful, but it is not a household pest and it will not infest a home. Cockroaches are the bigger concern. They travel through sewer lines and then walk across counters, dishes and food, and their droppings and shed skins are a known allergy and asthma trigger, especially for children.

Roaches also feed the food chain you do not want indoors. In Gilbert a steady supply of roaches and other insects can attract bark scorpions, which is why our scorpion control in Gilbert includes reducing the insects they hunt. If you are worried about bites specifically, our Queen Creek guide to cockroach bites explains what is and is not likely.

What Should You Do If You Find a Water Bug in Your House?

Identify it, then deal with the source. A single giant water bug near the back door is a one-time visitor: carry it out and turn off or swap the porch light that attracted it. A cockroach is a sign to look for a path in.

  • Run water in every unused drain once a week to keep the traps full.
  • Fit drain covers or stoppers in floor drains and rarely used tubs.
  • Seal gaps around pipes under sinks and at the water heater.
  • Keep irrigation and meter box lids closed and clear debris and mulch away from the slab.
  • Fix leaks under sinks and at outdoor hose bibs so roaches lose their water source.
  • Store pet food in sealed containers and do not leave it out overnight.

If you see roaches in more than one room, during the day, or several nights in a row, the source is likely in the sewer connection, wall voids or outdoor boxes, and store-bought sprays will not reach it.

Do roach sprays work on sewer roaches?

They kill the roach they hit, but the population that lives in the sewer and utility boxes keeps sending more. Lasting control comes from treating harborage outside, at entry points and in voids, combined with sealing and drain maintenance.

How Do We Get Rid of "Water Bugs" in Gilbert Homes?

We treat the roach population where it lives and closes the paths into the house. A typical visit through our pest control in Gilbert covers:

  1. Inspection: we confirm the species, then check drains, plumbing penetrations, the garage, the water heater area, and outdoor irrigation and meter boxes.
  2. Exterior treatment: perimeter and harborage treatment around the foundation, utility boxes and entry points.
  3. Interior treatment where needed: targeted products in voids and along the routes roaches use, not broad spraying of living areas.
  4. Exclusion advice: specific gaps and drains to seal or cover so fewer roaches make it inside.
  5. Follow-up: ongoing service keeps pressure on outdoor populations through the hot months.

Every service is backed by our 100% Money Back Guarantee *Terms and conditions apply. For more Gilbert-specific roach advice, read our Morrison Ranch roach elimination guide, and if you have seen roaches flying on hot nights, see whether cockroaches can fly.

Do Neighboring East Valley Cities See the Same Problem?

Yes. Sewer roaches and the "water bug" mix-up come up across the East Valley. We handle the same calls through pest control in Mesa, pest control in Chandler and pest control in Queen Creek, as well as in Tempe and San Tan Valley. The pattern is the same everywhere: the roaches come from below ground and from damp boxes outside, so the fix starts there.

Frequently Asked Questions About Water Bugs and Cockroaches

Is a water bug the same as a cockroach?

No. A true water bug is an aquatic insect that lives in ponds and lakes. But most insects people call water bugs indoors are American or Oriental cockroaches.

How do I know if it is a water bug or a roach?

Look at the antennae. Long, thread-like antennae mean cockroach. Short, hidden antennae with thick grasping front legs mean a true water bug.

Do water bugs bite?

True water bugs can bite painfully if handled. Cockroaches very rarely bite people.

Can water bugs infest a house?

True water bugs cannot live in a house and leave or die indoors. Cockroaches nicknamed water bugs can establish themselves in drains, voids and outdoor boxes around a home.

Why do I see water bugs at night?

Cockroaches are active at night and come out to feed, and true water bugs fly to outdoor lights after dark. Seeing roaches in daylight can point to a larger population.

Yes. We serve 85233, 85234, 85295, 85296, 85297 and 85298. Call (480) 422-8388 or request service online.
